2026: راديو دبنقا قالت وزارة الخارجية السودانية الاحد ان الحكومة اودعت شكوى ضد إثيوبيا لدى كل من مجلس الأمن ومجلس السلم والأمن الإفريقي، على خلفية اتهامات لدولة اثيوبيا المجاورة بالتورط في الاعتداء على مواقع وأعيان مدنية ومحطات كهرباء في عدد من ولايات السودان، تسببت في وقوع ضحايا مدنيين وتعطيل للخدمات الضرورية في البلاد وقالت الوزارة في بيان يوم الأحد، إن “حكومة السودان أرفقت كافة الوثائق والمستندات التي تؤكد استخدام الدعم السريع للأراضي الإثيوبية لإطلاق المسيرات الانتحارية والمزودة بالصواريخ، مستهدفة الأعيان المدنية والمرافق الحيوية”.أخبار السودان وشدد بيان الخارجية السودانية على أن استخدام الدعم السريع للأراضي الإثيوبية لاستهداف السودان يُعد عملاً عدائياً يضع إثيوبيا أمام القانون الدولي، ويحاسبها على انتهاكها للمادة (4) 2 من ميثاق الأمم المتحدة حسبما جاء في البيان وطالبت حكومة السودان بحسب البيان نظيرتها الإثيوبية بوقف هذه الأعمال العدائية، كما حثت المجتمع الدولي على القيام بدوره تجاه محاسبة ما اسماه بيان الخارجية “بالمليشيا الإرهابية” وتطبيق القانون الدولي على الحكومة الإثيوبية ولم يصدر تعقيب فوري من الحكومة الإثيوبية على بيان الخارجية السودانية. وتأتي هذه التطورات المتسارعة عقب هجمات بطائرات مسيّرة استهدفت 14 محطة لتوزيع الكهرباء في ولايات القضارف والخرطوم sudan.summary: قدمت وزارة الخارجية السودانية شكوى ضد إثيوبيا إلى مجلس الأمن ومجلس السلم والأمن الإفريقي، متهمة إياها بالتورط في هجمات على مواقع مدنية ومحطات كهرباء في عدة ولايات سودانية. وأكدت الحكومة السودانية أن هذه الهجمات، التي أسفرت عن وقوع ضحايا مدنيين وتعطيل الخدمات الأساسية، تمت باستخدام طائرات مسيرة انتحارية أُطلقت من الأراضي الإثيوبية. وأشارت الوزارة إلى أن هذه الأفعال تُعتبر عملاً عدائياً، مما يستوجب محاسبة إثيوبيا وفقاً للقانون الدولي. كما دعت الحكومة السودانية إثيوبيا إلى وقف هذه الأعمال، وحثت المجتمع الدولي على اتخاذ إجراءات ضد ما وصفته بـ"المليشيا الإرهابية". تأتي هذه التطورات بعد سلسلة من الهجمات التي استهدفت 14 محطة كهرباء، مما أدى إلى انقطاع التيار الكهربائي في عدة مناطق. لم يصدر أي رد من الحكومة الإثيوبية حتى الآن.

السودانية قوات الدعم السريع بالوقوف وراء تصعيد الهجمات بالطائرات المسيّرة - غيتي الخط تصاعد هجمات المسيّرات في السودان يطال محطات الكهرباء ومنشآت حيوية، وسط اتهامات لقوات الدعم السريع ومخاوف من تداعياتها على المدنيين. تتواصل جبهات الحرب في السودان على وقع تصاعد هجمات الطائرات المسيّرة، التي باتت تستهدف منشآت حيوية وبنية تحتية مدنية، بعدما طالت خلال أسبوع واحد محطات لتوزيع الكهرباء وتوليدها في عدد من الولايات. وتثير هذه الهجمات تساؤلات بشأن دوافعها والجهات المستفيدة منها، في وقت تتزايد فيه المخاوف من تداعياتها على حياة المدنيين والأوضاع الإنسانية. وتدخل الحرب المستمرة في السودان منذ أكثر من ثلاث سنوات مرحلة جديدة، تتصدر مشهدها هجمات المسيّرات التي لا تقتصر آثارها على المواقع العسكرية وخطوط الإمداد، بل تمتد إلى منشآت الطاقة والمدن التي تشهد استقرارًا نسبيًا، ما يهدد بإعادتها إلى دائرة انعدام الأمن وتعطيل مقومات الحياة فيها. هجمات المسيّرات في السودان تهدد حياة المدنيين وخلال أسبوع واحد، استهدفت هجمات بالطائرات المسيّرة محطات كهرباء في ولايات الخرطوم والجزيرة وسنار والقضارف ونهر النيل والبحر الأحمر، في تصعيد يطال البنية التحتية للطاقة، ويزيد من معاناة السكان. وفي أحدث هذه الهجمات، استهدفت مسيّرة مدينة الدبة ومحطة الكهرباء التحويلية فيها بالولاية الشمالية، شمالي البلاد. كما تعرضت محطة الكهرباء التحويلية في مدينة أبو حمد بولاية نهر النيل لهجوم مماثل، ما أدى إلى انقطاع الكهرباء عن المدينتين ودخولهما في ظلام دامس. ولا تقتصر تداعيات تصاعد استخدام المسيّرات على انقطاع التيار الكهربائي، إذ تسببت هجماتها في سقوط مئات الضحايا، ما دفع الأمم المتحدة إلى التحذير من تحول هذه الطائرات إلى أداة رئيسية لقتل المدنيين وتدمير مقومات الحياة في السودان. وأعرب الأمين العام للأمم المتحدة أنطونيو غوتيريش عن صدمته إزاء الحصيلة الكارثية للهجمات. منشآت الطاقة في السودان تتحول إلى أهداف لحرب المسيرات #الأخيرة https://t.co/GEUDVldbjE — التلفزيون العربي (@AlarabyTV) November 2, 2026 ويأتي الموقف الأممي في ظل اتساع نطاق استخدام المسيّرات خلال العام الجاري، بعدما تحولت من سلاح يستهدف المواقع العسكرية وخطوط الإمداد إلى مصدر متزايد للخسائر في صفوف المدنيين. ولم تعد الهجمات تقتصر على الأهداف العسكرية، بل امتدت إلى الأسواق وملاجئ النازحين والمستشفيات والمؤسسات التعليمية. اتهامات لقوات الدعم السريع بتوسيع هجمات المسيّرات وفي المقابل، تتهم الحكومة السودانية قوات الدعم السريع بالوقوف وراء تصعيد الهجمات بالطائرات المسيّرة، بالتزامن مع تحولات ميدانية تشهد تقدمًا للجيش في عدد من المحاور، ولا سيما في كردفان وغرب دارفور، فضلًا عن تعرض قوات الدعم السريع لهجمات بالمسيّرات في معاقلها الرئيسية. وتكتسب هذه الهجمات أهمية إضافية بالنظر إلى طبيعة المناطق المستهدفة، إذ تتركز على مدن تقع تحت سيطرة الحكومة السودانية وتشهد استقرارًا نسبيًا. ويرى مراقبون أن استهداف هذه المناطق قد يهدف إلى نقل أجواء الحرب وانعدام الأمن إليها، وإشاعة الخوف بين سكانها، بما يضع ضغوطًا إضافية على القيادة العسكرية والسياسية. إقرأ أيضاً سياسة - السودان السودان بين الحرب والحوار.. هل ينجح المسار السياسي في إنهاء القتال؟ وفي هذا السياق، حذر مستشار الحكومة السودانية مصلح الرشيدي من تداعيات استمرار الهجمات على الأمن والاستقرار، معتبرًا أن استهداف محطات الطاقة الكهربائية يمثل مسألة خطيرة. كما اتهم قوات الدعم السريع بالضلوع في مخطط أوسع يستهدف البلاد. وبينما تتواصل الهجمات على المنشآت الحيوية، يدخل النزاع السوداني منعطفًا جديدًا، في ظل اتهامات يوجهها الجيش السوداني إلى أطراف إقليمية بتأجيج الصراع، استديوهات لوسيل أن هذا الشعور بالهزيمة يدفعها إلى استهداف الخدمات الحيوية، وعلى رأسها محطات الكهرباء والبترول، بما في ذلك المحطات التحويلية التي تغذي ولايات السودان بالكهرباء من الخزانات الرئيسية. ميدان متخصصة محليات فيديو الحساب البث الحي فلسطين انتخابات أمريكا اليمن إيران أخبار السودان السودان يشكو إثيوبيا لدى مجلس الأمن ومجلس السلم الأفريقي 2 نوفمبر 2026 حفظ شارِكْ وقت القراءة: 3 دقائق آثار هجوم بطيران مسيّر نفذته قوات الدعم السريع في السودان (أسوشيتد برس) استمع 4:44 0:00 4:44 2:55 أعلن السودان الأحد إيداع شكوى ضد إثيوبيا لدى كل من مجلس الأمن الدولي ومجلس السلم والأمن الأفريقي على خلفية الاعتداء من داخل أراضيها على مواقع وأعيان مدنية ومحطات كهرباء في السودان. وأمس الأحد، قال مجلس السيادة السوداني إن أكثر من 180 طائرة مسيّرة تابعة لقوات الدعم السريع هاجمت السودان -خلال العام الجاري- انطلاقا من داخل الأراضي الإثيوبية. أخبار مقترحة السودان يتهم إثيوبيا بإطلاق 187 مسيّرة استهدفت أراضيه ويطالب بالتعويضات 15 محطة و9 ولايات.. كيف امتدت هجمات المسيّرات على شبكة الكهرباء السودانية خلال 10 أيام؟ وقالت الخارجية السودانية -في بيان- إن حكومة السودان أودعت شكوى ضد حكومة جمهورية إثيوبيا الفدرالية لدى كل من مجلس الأمن الدولي ومجلس السلم والأمن الأفريقي. وأضافت أن الشكوى تأتي على خلفية الاعتداء السافر من داخل الأراضي الإثيوبية على مواقع وأعيان مدنية ومحطات كهرباء في عدد من ولايات السودان، مما تسبب في وقوع ضحايا مدنيين وتعطيل للخدمات الضرورية للمواطنين. ووفقا للبيان، فقد أرفقت حكومة السودان كافة الوثائق والمستندات التي تؤكد استخدام مليشيا الدعم السريع المتمردة للأراضي الإثيوبية لإطلاق المسيرات الانتحارية المزودة بالصواريخ مستهدفة الأعيان المدنية والمرافق الحيوية. وقالت الخارجية السودانية -في بيانها- إن "استخدام المليشيا الإرهابية للأراضي الإثيوبية لاستهداف الأراضي السودانية يُعد عملاً عدائياً، يضع إثيوبيا أمام القانون الدولي ويحاسبها على انتهاكها للمادة (4) 2 من ميثاق الأمم المتحدة ". وتابع البيان أن حكومة السودان تطالب حكومة إثيوبيا بوقف هذه الأعمال العدائية ، كما تحث المجتمع الدولي على القيام بدوره تجاه محاسبة المليشيا الإرهابية وتطبيق القانون الدولي على الحكومة الإثيوبية. ولم يصدر تعقيب فوري من الحكومة الإثيوبية على بيان الخارجية السودانية. وتأتي هذه التطورات عقب هجمات بطائرات مسيّرة استهدفت 13 محطة كهرباء في الخرطوم و الجزيرة و سنار والقضارف منذ الاثنين الماضي. وتتهم الحكومة السودانية إثيوبيا بدعم قوات الدعم السريع وانطلاق الطائرات المسيرة من أراضيها، فيما تنفي إثيوبيا هذه الاتهامات وتقول إنها تحترم سيادة السودان على أراضيه. ومنذ أبريل/نيسان 2023، تحارب قوات الدعم السريع الجيش السوداني بسبب خلاف بشأن المرحلة الانتقالية، مما تسبب في مقتل عشرات آلاف السودانيين ونزوح نحو 13 مليونا. المصدر: الجزيرة + الأناضول حفظ شارِكْ حول هذه القصة السودان يتهم الجمركية، وسط حديث عن تقدم في المفاوضات وإمكانية التوصل إلى اتفاق قريب. مقتل 9 أشخاص إثر تحطم طائرة بولاية فلوريدا الأمريكية أوضحت السلطات الأمريكية أن الطائرة كانت في رحلة من تكساس إلى جزر الباهاما، ethiopia.content: Ethiopia’s Defence Modernization Signals New Era of Strategic Deterrence - ENA English - ENA Skip to Content Ethiopia’s Defence Modernization Signals New Era of Strategic Deterrence - ENA English Live: አማርኛ ትግርኛ Afaan Oromoo Af‑Soomaali Qafar Afa English Français عربي Politics Social Economy Sport Technology Environment Feature Videos About Us Ethiopia’s Defence Modernization Signals New Era of Strategic Deterrence 🔇Unmute By Staff Writer November 1 , 2026 (ENA) Ethiopia’s announcement of the acquisition of advanced Russian-made Su-35 fighter jets and plans to receive S-400 air defence systems marks a significant development in the country’s efforts to modernize its national defence capabilities, strengthen the protection of its airspace and reinforce its strategic deterrence. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed announced on October 28 in Moscow, Russia that Ethiopia had taken delivery of its first batch of Su-35 fighter jets under an agreement with Russia and would also receive four batteries of the S-400 air defence system. He described the development as a major milestone in the country’s efforts to strengthen national security, safeguard sovereignty and contribute to regional stability. The announcement, made during the Prime Minister’s visit to Moscow for the Third Russia–Africa Summit, also underscored the growing defence cooperation between Ethiopia and Russia. Beyond Military Acquisition: A Strategic Investment in National Security The acquisition represents more than the addition of advanced military equipment to Ethiopia’s arsenal. It reflects a broader effort to build a modern defence force capable of responding to evolving security challenges and protecting the country's national interests. The Su-35, a fourth-generation-plus multirole fighter, is designed to undertake air-superiority and air-to-ground missions. Its advanced radar, manoeuvrability and weapons systems provide capabilities for airspace surveillance, interception and a range of combat operations. The planned acquisition of the Russian-made S-400 system would add another dimension to Ethiopia’s air defence architecture. Designed to engage aircraft, cruise missiles and other aerial threats, the system is intended to provide long-range air defence capabilities and strengthen the protection of strategic assets. Together, these platforms could expand Ethiopia’s capacity to monitor and defend its airspace. However, their effectiveness will depend not only on the equipment itself but also on trained personnel, maintenance systems, logistics, command-and-control infrastructure and the ability to integrate different defence capabilities. Deterrence as an Instrument of Peace The strategic significance of military modernization extends beyond battlefield capabilities. A credible defence posture can serve as a deterrent by raising the potential costs of aggression and discouraging threats before they escalate into conflict. Prime Minister Abiy has emphasized this principle, noting that military preparedness is not simply about fighting wars but also about preventing them. For Ethiopia, strengthening defence readiness is closely connected to protecting its sovereignty, territorial integrity and national development interests. The objective, as articulated by the government, is to build the capacity to safeguard peace and security while reducing vulnerability to external threats. This approach places deterrence within a broader national security framework in which military preparedness is intended to support stability rather than confrontation. Regional Security and the Horn of Africa Ethiopia’s defence modernization carries significance beyond its national borders, particularly given its strategic position in the Horn of Africa and its extensive economic and security interests across the wider Red Sea region. As a landlocked country with a large population and substantial dependence on regional trade and transport corridors, Ethiopia has important interests in the security of its airspace, critical infrastructure and cross-border economic connections. The evolving security environment in the Horn of Africa, together with the growing use of drones, precision-guided weapons and other emerging military technologies, has increased the importance of modern surveillance, air defence and rapid-response capabilities. In this context, Ethiopia’s investment in advanced fighter aircraft and air defence systems reflects an effort to adapt its defence posture to changing regional and technological realities. At the same time, military modernization alone cannot guarantee regional stability. Sustainable peace also requires diplomatic engagement, confidence-building, respect for national sovereignty and stronger regional cooperation. A credible deterrent is most effective when complemented by constructive relations with neighbouring countries and regional institutions. Building a Modern and Sustainable Defence Force The acquisition of advanced platforms also places greater importance on the institutional and technological foundations of national defence. Operating sophisticated fighter aircraft and integrated air defence systems requires specialized training, reliable maintenance facilities, technical expertise, secure supply chains and sustained investment in personnel development. The Ethiopian National Defence Force (ENDF) has made significant strides in expanding its military capabilities through the acquisition of modern and sophisticated weaponry, reflecting an ambitious effort to transform its defence posture. Beyond conventional military capabilities, the ENDF is increasingly moving towards a technology-driven defence model, seeking to integrate artificial intelligence, cyber operations, digital warfare and advanced surveillance technologies into its military operations. This transition reflects the changing nature of modern warfare, where technological superiority, real-time intelligence and integrated command-and-control systems are becoming increasingly important. However, building a modern and technologically advanced military requires more than acquiring sophisticated weapons systems. It also demands sustained investment in specialized training, technical expertise, maintenance infrastructure, logistics, research and development, and institutional capacity to operate and sustain these capabilities over the long term. Strengthening these foundations will be essential to translating military modernization into lasting operational readiness and strategic self-reliance. The development also highlights the importance of strengthening domestic technical expertise and reducing dependence on external support wherever possible. Building such capabilities is essential to ensuring that military modernization translates into sustainable national defence readiness. Sovereignty, Security and the Pursuit of Peace Ethiopia’s latest defence acquisitions form part of a broader national effort to strengthen its security institutions and respond to an increasingly complex regional environment. The delivery of the Su-35 fighter jets and the planned arrival of the S-400 systems signal an expansion of the country’s defence ambitions and its military cooperation with Russia. Ultimately, the significance of this modernization will be measured not simply by the sophistication of the equipment acquired, but by the country's ability to translate those capabilities into effective national defence, strategic resilience and a more secure regional environment. For Ethiopia, the central objective remains the protection of sovereignty and the preservation of peace. A modern, capable and sustainable defence force, complemented by diplomacy and regional cooperation, can play an important role in safeguarding national interests and creating the security conditions necessary for long-term development. © Ethiopian News Agency 2023 Hidden

Published 21 hours ago on November 1, 2026 By Kulu Media News Desk A speaker reads a statement alongside two other men during an apparent Alliance for Survival press briefing. Photo credit: TMC/ Screenshot & Illustrated by Kulu Media The Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, a coalition of armed and political opposition groups, has issued a new statement calling for coordinated action against Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government and outlining its position on Ethiopia’s political and security crises. In a four-page statement dated October 31, 2026, and shared on Facebook , the coalition, also known as the Alliance for Survival, accused the federal government of deepening the country’s political divisions, prolonging armed conflicts and failing to protect civilians. The alliance argued that Ethiopia’s current challenges require fundamental political change rather than measures undertaken by the existing administration. It presented cooperation among opposition organizations and communities as central to achieving that objective. The statement blamed the government for what the coalition described as widespread insecurity, displacement, human rights violations and deteriorating economic conditions. These allegations represent the alliance’s position and have not all been independently verified. The coalition also reiterated its opposition to the current federal administration and emphasized the need for a political arrangement that would protect the rights, security and participation of Ethiopia’s different communities. Its statement called for broader cooperation among political organizations, community representatives and other groups opposed to the government. It also addressed members of Ethiopia’s security institutions, urging them to reconsider their role in the country’s political and military conflicts. The alliance has previously identified the replacement of the current government and the establishment of an inclusive transitional administration as central objectives. The latest declaration continues that political position, although it does not establish that a transition has been agreed upon or that the coalition has secured additional territory or military support. The Alliance for Survival emerged in September 2026 as a coalition bringing together organizations with different political backgrounds and regional interests, including the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), the Amhara Fano National Movement and the Oromo Liberation Army. Its formation drew attention because some participating organizations have historically pursued competing political objectives or fought on opposing sides of earlier conflicts. Their cooperation reflects a shared opposition to the federal government, but does not necessarily mean that their wider political differences have been resolved. The new statement comes amid renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia, including confrontations involving TPLF-aligned forces, the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) and the Tigray Peace Force (TPF). Recent developments in Tigray have included the reported reentry of TPLF forces into Rama , followed by reports of drone strike damage in the area . The conflict has raised questions about the alliance’s military coordination and the extent to which its members can pursue a common strategy despite their differing political priorities. The declaration appears intended to reaffirm the coalition’s continued political cooperation and appeal for wider support. However, the statement does not independently establish a new joint military offensive, a formal agreement with additional organizations or a change in the balance of forces on the ground. No new response from the Ethiopian federal government to the October 31 statement had been independently verified at the time of writing. The alliance’s declaration adds to the political uncertainty surrounding Ethiopia’s continuing conflicts, although the practical implications of its latest calls remain unclear. Addressing the Third Russia–Africa Summit in Moscow, Abiy said the proposed Ethiopia nuclear power plant would diversify the country’s electricity supply, which currently relies heavily on hydropower. “With Russia, we are moving toward our first nuclear power plant in line with the safety standards of the International Atomic Energy Agency,” Abiy said in his summit speech , published on his official YouTube channel. The prime minister said nuclear technology could also help reduce agricultural food losses and support healthcare, including cancer treatment. He emphasized that cooperation with Moscow should develop Ethiopian expertise to operate and regulate nuclear facilities. The remarks come as Ethiopia seeks to diversify its electricity generation beyond hydropower, which remains vulnerable to variations in rainfall and reservoir inflows. Earlier this year, Ethiopian Electric Power reported a 20 percent reduction in water inflows linked to El Niño conditions, prompting revisions to its electricity generation and revenue targets. Ethiopia’s nuclear ambitions have been under development for several years. The country signed an intergovernmental nuclear cooperation agreement with Russia in 2019, followed by additional cooperation roadmaps. In March 2026, the Ethiopian Nuclear Energy Commission and Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom signed a strategic roadmap covering nuclear energy development. According to World Nuclear News, Ethiopia is considering two reactors with a combined generating capacity of approximately 2,400 megawatts. However, the project remains at the planning stage, with potential sites requiring further assessment. Abiy did not announce a construction start date, final financing agreement or completion timetable during his Moscow address. The prime minister identified food security, energy and knowledge as Ethiopia’s three principal development priorities. On agriculture, he called for Russian cooperation in farm machinery and agricultural processing industries to increase domestic production and strengthen food security. He said Ethiopia wanted to move beyond producing raw agricultural commodities by expanding industries capable of processing harvested products. Abiy also announced that Ethiopia is establishing the Medemer University of Artificial Intelligence in Addis Ababa and invited Russian universities and research institutions to participate in teaching and research. “An African researcher should be able to create tools in the language of our people,” he said, emphasizing that African institutions should determine how artificial intelligence systems use their data. The proposed university forms part of Ethiopia’s broader technological development ambitions. At the recent Tana High-Level Forum, Abiy also outlined the country’s Digital Ethiopia 2030 strategy , highlighting digital infrastructure, artificial intelligence and data governance as priorities for economic development. The prime minister said scientific cooperation should produce practical economic benefits rather than remain limited to academic exchanges. He invited Russian enterprises to establish joint ventures in Ethiopia’s special economic zones, particularly in pharmaceutical manufacturing and machinery production. Such investments, he said, could supply markets across Africa through the African Continental Free Trade Area. Abiy also called for improved payment arrangements between Ethiopia and Russia to make bilateral trade simpler and less expensive. His proposals came as the two countries continued expanding diplomatic, economic and military cooperation. During the Moscow summit, Abiy held bilateral discussions with Russian President Vladimir Putin on nuclear energy, healthcare, trade and other areas of mutual interest. The talks followed Ethiopia’s recent announcement concerning the acquisition of Russian military aircraft and air-defence equipment. On October 28, Kulu Media reported that Ethiopia announced new Russian Su-35 fighter jets amid renewed military tensions in the Horn of Africa. The latest summit discussions indicate that Ethiopia is seeking cooperation with Moscow across both civilian and defence sectors. Abiy also proposed that Addis Ababa host a future Russia–Africa Summit when the gathering next takes place on the African continent. He said the Ethiopian capital, which hosts the African Union headquarters, would be honored to welcome the meeting. However, he did not announce that Addis Ababa had been formally selected as the venue. The prime minister urged participating countries to adopt an action plan containing clear responsibilities and implementation timelines. He said international cooperation should translate diplomatic commitments into practical results. On international affairs, Abiy reaffirmed Ethiopia’s support for negotiated solutions, African-led mediation and consistent application of the United Nations Charter. His remarks came amid continuing Ethiopia-Eritrea tensions , with international partners urging restraint and diplomatic engagement to prevent a broader regional conflict. Abiy did not directly address the dispute with Eritrea in the supplied summit speech. Reflecting on historical relations, the prime minister recalled a Russian medical mission that assisted wounded Ethiopians following the Battle of Adwa in 1896. He said the mission translated a medical guide into Amharic, presenting the initiative as an early example of scientific cooperation between the two countries. Abiy also noted that his book Medemer had been translated into Russian, describing the exchange of knowledge as a symbol of the longstanding relationship. The speech concluded with a call for stronger cooperation based on sovereignty, technological capability and shared economic development. For Ethiopia, the proposed nuclear power plant, artificial intelligence university and expanded industrial partnerships represent central elements of the government’s long-term development agenda. However, the financing, construction timetable and implementation arrangements for the nuclear project remain to be finalized. Continue Reading Ethiopia Breaking: Ethiopia Expands Airpower With 12 Russian Jets as Regional Tensions Rise Published 4 days ago on October 28, 2026 By Kulu Media News Desk Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed stands in front of military fighter aircraft at an airbase. Photo Credit: PM Abiy Ahmed Ali/Facebook Ethiopia has announced the arrival of 12 advanced Russian Su-35 fighter jets, marking a major expansion of its military airpower as renewed fighting in Tigray and worsening relations with Eritrea raise security concerns across the Horn of Africa. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed announced the delivery on October 28, 2026, saying the aircraft were supplied under an existing defence agreement with Russia. He also confirmed plans for Ethiopia to receive four batteries of Russia’s S-400 air-defence system, although no delivery date was announced. According to Ethiopia’s state-affiliated Fana Media Corporation , Abiy described the arrival of the aircraft as an important step in strengthening national security and protecting Ethiopia’s sovereignty. The prime minister said Russian President Vladimir Putin had helped accelerate the delivery, allowing Ethiopia to receive the fighter jets one year earlier than originally scheduled. The announcement coincided with Abiy’s visit to Russia for the third Russia–Africa Summit, where defence cooperation has become a prominent element of relations between Addis Ababa and Moscow. The Su-35 is a Russian-built, twin-engine multirole fighter aircraft designed for air-to-air combat and air-to-ground missions. Its advanced radar, maneuverability and weapons capabilities could expand the Ethiopian Air Force’s operational options. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and Ethiopian and Russian officials pose for a group photograph in front of a fighter aircraft during a military aviation event. Photo Credit: PM Abiy Ahmed Ali / Facebook The planned S-400 acquisition would add another dimension to Ethiopia’s military modernization. The Russian-developed system is designed to detect and engage aircraft, missiles and other airborne threats at considerable distances. However, the government has not disclosed the value of the agreement, the expected arrival date of the S-400 batteries or where the newly acquired aircraft will be stationed. In its October 28 report , Reuters said Russian state-owned defence conglomerate Rostec had not immediately responded to a request for comment. The aircraft delivery announcement comes during a particularly sensitive period for Ethiopia’s security environment. Fighting involving the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF), TPLF-aligned forces and the Tigray Peace Force (TPF) has intensified in northern Ethiopia since September, while relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara have deteriorated sharply. The Ethiopian government has accused Eritrea of supporting TPLF-aligned forces and interfering in Ethiopia’s internal security affairs. Eritrea has rejected accusations of involvement and has made counterclaims concerning Ethiopian military intentions. Earlier this month, Ethiopia formally accused Eritrea of an invasion , alleging that Eritrean troops had advanced into northern Ethiopia. The allegations remain disputed. Ethiopian military chief Field Marshal Berhanu Jula also recently accused Eritrea, Egypt and Sudan of supporting TPLF-aligned forces, including through alleged weapons transfers. Those specific allegations have not been independently verified. The new aircraft could strengthen Ethiopia’s capacity to defend its airspace and conduct military operations, although their immediate operational readiness and deployment arrangements remain unknown. There is no verified evidence that the newly delivered Su-35 fighters have been deployed in the current fighting or assigned to operations against Eritrea. The acquisition nevertheless carries regional significance because Ethiopia and Eritrea remain locked in a confrontation involving border security, political alliances and Ethiopia’s long-standing interest in reliable access to the Red Sea. International concern about a broader conflict has increased. The United States recently warned of wider war , urging restraint as tensions between the two countries continued. Russia has also indicated a willingness to facilitate discussions between Ethiopia and Eritrea if both governments agree, but no confirmed bilateral negotiations have emerged from the Moscow summit. Ethiopia and Russia have maintained military relations for decades, including cooperation involving combat aircraft, defence equipment and technical training. The latest announcement signals a further strengthening of those ties at a time when Ethiopia is seeking to modernize its armed forces while navigating internal conflict and regional diplomatic pressure. For now, the confirmed government announcement concerns the delivery of 12 Su-35 fighter jets. The four S-400 air-defence batteries remain part of a future delivery commitment, with their schedule and deployment locations undisclosed. Photos shared by him on social media show him taking part in military exercises alongside ministers, deputy ministers and heads of government institutions at the Hurso military training centre. The move is unusual in Ethiopia, where senior civilian government officials are rarely seen undergoing military training. Those taking part include Speaker of the House of Federation Muferiat Kamil, Finance Minister Fitsum Assefa and Health Minister Mekdes Daba. It is unclear when the training began or how long it is expected to last. In his post, the prime minister, who is known as Abiy, said Ethiopia's ambition to achieve universal prosperity required its leadership to be physically fit, morally strong and intellectually capable. He said military institutions offered valuable lessons in discipline, patriotism, teamwork, accountability and leadership. "Soldiers have targets while civilians have goals. The objective of both is victory," he said, adding that combining military and civilian disciplines would help create a generation capable of achieving both. Abiy argued that military training could help develop leaders with a strong sense of purpose, responsibility and the ability to work together towards common objectives. The training comes as Ethiopia faces multiple security challenges, including continued fighting in parts of the northern Tigray region, conflict in Amhara and insecurity in Oromia. It also takes place amid heightened tensions with neighbouring Eritrea, with concerns over the possibility of renewed conflict between the two countries. Abiy has previously emphasised military preparedness and national development as central to his government's ambitions. ethiopia.content: The Red Sea Chokehold: Why Maritime Access Is an Existential Question for Ethiopia – HORN REVIEW Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us Search Home About Us Team Research and Analysis Horn Geopolitics Global Politics Ethiopia and the World Publications News Reports and Articles Horn Review Journal Articles Horn Review Magazine Report Amharic Publications Amharic News Reports and Articles Amharic Research and Analysis Amharic Ethiopia and the World Amharic Global Politics Amharic Horn Geopolitics Amharic Horn Review Journal Articles Amharic horn review magazine Amharic Report News and Events Contact Us 2026-10-31 The Red Sea Chokehold: Why Maritime Access Is an Existential Question for Ethiopia 0 Comments For a landlocked nation, maritime access is rarely a matter of simple commerce; it is an existential variable that dictates economic survival, sovereign autonomy, and strategic viability. When a country’s geographic bottleneck is policed by a deeply militarized dictator with no clear economic vision, the resulting friction transcends ordinary bilateral disputes, elevating infrastructure into a primary casus belli. No regional dynamic illustrates this geopolitical chokehold more acutely than the volatile relationship between Ethiopia and Eritrea. For decades, international observers have viewed Ethiopia’s quest for a seaport through a purely commercial lens, equating it as a matter of trade balances, shipping tariffs, and economic optimization. But as the Red Sea rapidly transforms into one of the most volatile, hyper-militarized maritime corridors on the planet, this perspective is dangerously obsolete. For Ethiopia, a nation of over 130 million people, permanent and reliable access to the sea is no longer just an economic aspiration. It is an existential imperative for national security and survival. This assertion makes sense if viewed critically beyond a shallow attempt to reduce the looming danger to a simple expansionist ambition. One must always reconsider the facts on the ground while analyzing the conundrum in the Horn of Africa. Ethiopia, a country that is only 60 kms from the Red sea, is the most populous landlocked country in the world, whose significant portion of the population is youth and in active pursuit of job opportunities. According to recent IMF reports, the country is also home to the fastest growing economy in the entire sub-Saharan Africa. This is not merely a statistical trivia point framed for political purpose; rather it is a profound strategic vulnerability. Every piece of medicine, fuel, and technology that enters the country, and every single product exported to sustain its economy, depends entirely on the political whims and stability of its coastal neighbors. Currently, Ethiopia relies on Djibouti for roughly 95% of its trade, paying upwards between $1.5 to $2 billion annually in port fees. This single door dependency is an economic chokehold. No sovereign state can safely anchor its future on a single corridor that is vulnerable to external influences. For countries like Ethiopia, the highly volatile security situation in its surrounding doubles down the impact, without mentioning the challenges associated with the growing number of military bases in the region. Should political instability or hostile foreign influence freeze the docks of Djibouti, the Ethiopian economy would collapse triggering an internal humanitarian catastrophe of unprecedented scale. This is what makes Ethiopia’s concern undeniably legitimate and fuels its determination to address what it perceives as an existential threat through any means available. Just as a drowning person instinctively tries every possible option to stay afloat. A nation of 130 million people cannot be trapped in a geographic cage at the mercy of volatile, highly militarized autocratic coastal regime. A stable, secure Horn of Africa is impossible if its largest engine of population and economic powerhouse is kept in a state of permanent anxiety and artificial suffocation. Securing a permanent and dependable commercial and naval gateway to the Red Sea is not an empire building ambition or a luxury. For Ethiopia, it is becoming a simple, legitimate right to breath and it is the only way to bring peace and security in the entire Horn. Encirclement, Exclusion, and Ethiopia’s Security Imperative The urgency underpinning Ethiopia’s vulnerability has been sharply accelerated by the growing securitization of the Red Sea. What was once an open global trade route has become an arena for geopolitical chess, dominated by state coalitions and non-state actors from near and afar. Global and regional powers increasingly framing the vital corridor as a critical national security priority rather than just a commercial shipping lane. Driven by the need to safeguard chokepoints like the Bab el Mandab Strait from asymmetric threats, piracy, and regional conflicts, world powers have rapidly expanded their footprint through a dense concentration of military bases along the coastline. Djibouti has become the primary epicenter of this militarization, uniquely hosting overlapping naval facilities for both the United States (Camp Lemonnier) and China, alongside presence from France and Japan. Concurrently, nations like Russia have sought access, while regional actors such as Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Turkye, and Israel are all vying for influence via port logistics and security pacts along the broader Horn of Africa. While these external militaries provide short-term protection for international shipping, their crowding presence has ultimately transformed the Red Sea into a complex arena of overlapping geopolitical rivalries and proxy vulnerabilities, weakening the prospects for a self-sustaining regional security framework and brutally doubling down on Ethiopia’s unique vulnerability. As if these threats are not enough, Ethiopia is alarmed by a recent development of an architectural web of alliances orchestrated explicitly to isolate it from its own geographic backyard. The creation of the El Alamein Joint Declaration by Egypt, Eritrea, and Somalia is not as a routine diplomatic pact, but a deliberate strategy of encirclement. By codifying that Red Sea governance belongs exclusively to coastal states, regional adversaries seek to permanently deny landlocked Ethiopia a seat at the table. Proofing that the danger felt by Ethiopia is eminent beyond perception and this could potentially leave the country to consider every option to break the chokehold before it is too late. The action Ethiopia should take would be determined based on the scale and level of threats the country is faced with, as the end justifies the means. This encirclement is amplified by Egypt’s aggressive forward deployment rhetoric in the region. Driven by tensions over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), Cairo is trying to weaponize Ethiopia’s landlocked status by forming tight military and logistical alliances with Eritrea and other states bordering Ethiopia. From the Ethiopian perspective, it is quite clear. Hostile foreign militaries are aspiring to setting up base camps right on its borders, holding the keys to the very maritime gates that feed the Ethiopian population. This is a recuring dangerous move. Previously, when multinational coalitions form to protect Red Sea shipping lines from asymmetric threats like piracy and militant groups, Ethiopia is routinely excluded. Addis Ababa is being forced to watch from the sidelines while its primary economic lifeblood is policed by an alliance sympathetic to its rivals. It is profoundly naïve to expect Ethiopia to remain passive while such a perilous scheme is being orchestrated to threaten the lives of its entire population and its very survival. This reality underscores Ethiopia’s existential need to secure a reliable maritime corridor through which it can establish dependable port services and maintain a sovereign naval capability. Such a capability is essential to safeguard its national interests, protect its flag-bearing vessels, and guarantee its unhindered right to innocent passage under international law. Ethiopia has consistently expressed its preference for cooperation and has repeatedly advanced frameworks centered on mutual economic integration, shared prosperity, and regional interdependence. However, while Ethiopia remains committed to peaceful collaboration, coastal states, particularly Eritrea, should recognize that legal technicalities or strategies aimed at regional containment cannot serve as sustainable solutions to a matter that directly concerns the livelihood, security, and future of such burgeoning population. When the survival and long-term interests of the entire nation is at stake, it is unrealistic to expect Ethiopia to remain passive. It will undoubtedly pursue all the necessary strategic measures to secure its legitimate access to the Red Sea and protect its vital national interests. In doing so, it will ensure that its sovereignty, security, and economic future are safeguarded both on land and at sea. In conclusion, Ethiopia’s demand for access to the sea must be understood by its neighbouring countries as a legitimate strategic and economic and security concerns that deserves serious, constructive, and peaceful consideration. Why would Ethiopia’s quest to establish a military base along the Red Sea coast be considered unacceptable when countries from far beyond the region already maintain military bases and enjoy strategic access to the same coastline? Is it just to deny a neighbouring country with vital security and economic interests in the region an opportunity to negotiate such access, while external powers are permitted to establish a military presence there? The issue should not be approached through double standards or geopolitical rivalries, but through constructive dialogue, mutual respect, and negotiated arrangements that uphold the sovereignty of coastal states while addressing Ethiopia’s legitimate interests. IGAD and the African Union must urgently take their leadership responsibilities by facilitating inclusive regional dialogue and developing a practical framework that addresses Ethiopia’s legitimate aspirations while safeguarding the legitimate interests of neighbouring states. External actors outside the Horn of Africa should be discouraged from pursuing their agendas by fostering hostility and division, rather than promoting cooperation, dialogue, and regional stability. The international community, including the United Nations and other influential partners, should also intensify diplomatic engagement and support a negotiated settlement before the situation deteriorates into a dangerous confrontation with far reaching consequences for the Horn of Africa and beyond. The time to act is now: through timely diplomacy, mutual understanding, and political courage, regional leaders and international stakeholders can transform a potential source of conflict into an opportunity for cooperation, shared prosperity, and lasting peace. Failure to act decisively today risks allowing tensions to spiral into a devastating conflict that the region and the wider world can ill afford. What next? Wikimedia Commons A false-color image of the area surrounding the coastal city of Assab and the Red Sea coast, based on satellite imagery data captured on 23 October 2019. The port of Assab and the risk of an Ethiopia-Eritrea war Amgad Fareid Eltayeb last update on 30 Oct 2026 The dispute between Ethiopia and Eritrea over the Red Sea port of Assab now extends well beyond that of a maritime facility or outlet for international trade. It reflects a structural contradiction between two states with a shared history but divided on issues like sovereignty, security, borders, and the state itself. For Ethiopia, Assab embodies its historical loss of direct access to the sea. This is a growing strategic concern, with the country’s population and economy both having expanded. For Eritrea, the port is a key and inseparable part of its sovereignty, won through a long war of independence. Thus, the port mixes economic interests with domestic power struggles, regional alliances, and foreign intervention, particularly in a region already afflicted by weak state institutions and protracted armed conflicts. The modern roots of the crisis lie in Italian colonial expansion in the 19th century. Italian control of Assab began in 1869 through the Rubattino shipping company, which acquired the right to administer the port from local authorities. Administration passed to the Italian state in 1882, and Assab subsequently became part of Italian Eritrea, formally established as a colony in 1890. With the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869, this was a time of intensifying European competition for ports and trade routes through the Red Sea. Italy lost control of East Africa in 1941, when Assab and the rest of Eritrea came under British occupation and administration. Following the Second World War, Eritrea’s future administration was debated. On 2 December 1950, the UN General Assembly adopted Resolution 390, recommending the establishment of a federation between Eritrea and Ethiopia. The arrangement came into effect in 1952. It recognised Ethiopia’s legitimate need for access to the sea, and granted autonomy to Eritrea (with its own legislative, executive and judicial institutions responsible for internal affairs) within a federation under the sovereignty of the Ethiopian Crown. The resolution did not grant Ethiopia permanent ownership of Assab as a separate sovereign possession, but it went beyond a commercial agreement between two independent states by establishing a federation with sovereign authority at the federal level, defined powers, and Eritrean autonomy. These legal distinctions remain essential to assessing the competing claims surrounding Assab today. Emperor Haile Selassie gradually undermined Eritrea’s autonomous institutions before abolishing the federal system and fully annexing the territory in 1962. A year earlier, Eritrea’s armed struggle for independence had already begun. The Ethiopian Empire fell in the revolution of 1974, and the military regime of Mengistu Haile Mariam reasserted centralised control through force. Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) fighters arrive after eight hours of walking in Mekele, the capital of the Tigray region, Ethiopia, on 29 June 2021. Alliances and interests Opposition to his rule fostered cooperation between the Eritrean People’s Liberation Front (EPLF) and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which was waging a parallel campaign to overthrow the regime. Their common struggle contributed to Mengistu’s defeat in 1991, although the alliance concealed a fundamental difference between their political ambitions: the Eritrean movement sought to establish an independent state, while the Tigrayan movement aimed to overthrow the regime and restructure power within Ethiopia. A common enemy had united them, but victory exposed their conflicting visions of statehood. Eritrea gained independence in 1993 following a popular referendum endorsed by Ethiopia’s new government, then led by Meles Zenawi, and it was recognised by the international community. Independence made Ethiopia landlocked, losing its direct access to the Red Sea. Yet this did not disappear overnight. The country continued to use Assab under arrangements agreed with Eritrea, until mounting economic, territorial and political disputes culminated in the 1998–2000 war. This ended with the Algiers Agreement, followed by the boundary commission’s ruling in 2002. Relations between the two countries remained hostile and Ethiopia shifted almost all its maritime trade to Djibouti. Subsequent demographic and economic developments have sharpened the consequences. Ethiopia now has 135 million people, a growing industrial economy, and a thirst for international trade, but with almost all its foreign trade passing through Djibouti, it depends heavily on a single transit route. That dependence creates genuine economic vulnerabilities. Sign up for our Weekly Newsletter Get the best of Majalla, straight to your inbox. Your newsletter subscriptions are subject to Al Majalla privacy policy and terms and conditions . Ethiopia has 135 million people, a growing industrial base, and a thirst for international trade, but almost all trade depends on a single transit route through Djibouti 'Existential necessity' It is not surprising that a country of Ethiopia's size should want to diversify its maritime outlets and secure reliable access to global markets, but however legitimate its economic needs may be, they confer no sovereign entitlement to another country's territory. The right of access to the sea is fundamentally different from the right to a coastline, just as facilitating trade is distinct from redrawing borders. Since October 2023, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has increasingly presented access to the Red Sea as an existential necessity, bound up with the country's future and security. His rhetoric has extended beyond improving commercial transit arrangements to demands for sovereign maritime access and naval capabilities. He invoked history to portray the loss of Ethiopia's coastline as a historical wrong that now needed to be corrected. This rhetoric has coincided with severe domestic crises, particularly in the northern regions of Tigray, Amhara, and Oromia. In January 2024, Ethiopia signed a memorandum of understanding with local authorities in Somaliland, a coastal region of Somalia that wants to break away. The proposed arrangement envisaged a stretch of coastline and the establishment of a naval facility in exchange for Ethiopian recognition of Somaliland's independence. Somalia's federal government rejected the agreement as a violation of its sovereignty, triggering tensions. Mediation by Türkiye produced the Ankara Declaration in December 2024, which acknowledged the possibility of Ethiopia securing sustainable commercial access to the sea under Somali sovereignty, without granting it a sovereign coastal outlet. In December 2025, Israel (which also wants Red Sea access) became the first UN member state to recognise Somaliland. Ethiopia's attempt to obtain sovereign maritime access through the Somali coast stalled, which brought renewed attention to the port of Assab, which occupies a distinctive place in Ethiopia's political memory. Somaliland President Abdirahman Abdullahi Mohamed during a press conference with Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar at the Presidential Palace in Hargeisa, 6 January 2026. Collapsing rapprochement The rapprochement between Ethiopia and Eritrea that began in 2018 was now collapsing. The reconciliation between Addis Ababa and Asmara had developed into a military alliance against the TPLF during the 2020-22 war, but the Pretoria Agreement, which ended that conflict, was subsequently signed without Eritrea's participation, creating a deep rift between the two countries. With no lasting framework for shared economic interests and mutual security guarantees, relations depended on a convergence of interests and calculations regarding domestic adversaries. As the arrangements underpinning Pretoria unravelled, Eritrea developed ties to the TPLF, despite them having fought so bitterly just a few years earlier. In September 2026, large-scale fighting resumed in Tigray. Ethiopian soldiers advanced, capturing Mekelle, the regional capital, before moving towards the Eritrean border. Thus began the latest and most dangerous phase. Addis Ababa and Asmara severed diplomatic relations and accused each other of military interference, support for armed groups, and aggression. Ethiopia invoked Article 51 of the UN Charter to justify measures it said it was taking in self-defence. Eritrea accused Ethiopia of using these claims as a pretext for seizing Assab. Military movements and mounting threats on both sides have now heightened the risk of war. This escalation cannot be understood in isolation. Foreign states have an interest in the Horn of Africa and seek to exploit state weaknesses. Ethiopia maintains close ties with the United Arab Emirates, which has economic and military influence in the ports of the region and across regional supply networks. Israel's recognition of Somaliland also signalled support for Ethiopia's ambitions to secure maritime access there. For Sudan, which has been ravaged by an ongoing civil war, the prospect of fighting between Ethiopia and Eritrea poses a direct threat. The Sudanese Armed Forces are fighting the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia, which now controls the giant Darfur region in western Sudan. The RSF supply network is said to include the UAE, but Abu Dhabi denies it. The International Crisis Group cites reports that RSF forces are stationed in the Benishangul-Gumuz region near the border and launch attacks from there into Sudan's Blue Nile region. Should war break out, the militarisation of the border, the flow of weapons and fighters, and further waves of displacement would compound these dangers, adding to the burden on Sudan. Any Ethiopia-Eritrea confrontation would therefore draw in overlapping conflicts and foreign actors. The harbour of Port Sudan on the Red Sea on 24 February 2014. It is Sudan's main seaport and source of 90% of its international trade. Dangers of escalation The maritime trade routes around the Horn of Africa are some of the world's busiest and most sensitive, as they intersect with the strategic interests of regional and global powers. Any extension of hostilities towards Eritrea's coastline would increase the risks to ports and shipping, drive up transport and insurance costs, and add more instability in a maritime corridor already suffering the repercussions of the civil war in Yemen. The African Union has a particular responsibility to turn its calls for restraint into urgent diplomatic action. It could reopen communication channels between Addis Ababa and Asmara, establish verifiable arrangements to prevent military clashes along the border, and support the resumption of a political process to address the conflict in Tigray. Regional governments could likewise approach the crisis as a shared threat to stability, rather than an opportunity to alter the balance of power in their favour. Saudi Arabia and Türkiye could help reduce tensions, forge understandings, and safeguard security in the Red Sea, but foreign powers supplying weapons must also commit to ending any military and financial assistance that fuels confrontation. Some call for peace while supplying the means to wage war. There is no inherent legal conflict between Ethiopia's right of access to the sea and Eritrea's sovereignty over its territory. International law recognises the legitimate interests and transit rights of landlocked states, while granting them no right to seize the territory of coastal countries. Respect for borders inherited at independence remains a cornerstone of the African regional order. Together with the prohibition on the use of force enshrined in the UN Charter, this principle places clear limits on territorial claims. A boatman transports visitors along a shore near the old port of Massawa—located 60 kilometers from the Eritrean capital—including civilians arriving from Ethiopia to visit Eritrea's Dahlak Islands. Contractual agreements, joint investments, and reciprocal security arrangements could provide practical solutions to the question of maritime access without reopening disputes over sovereignty. Ethiopia and Eritrea have already demonstrated that Eritrean independence can coexist with Ethiopian use of the port of Assab. Geography did not end that arrangement; it collapsed because political and security understandings between the two countries broke down. Renewing cooperation will require more than another port agreement; it will demand measures to address mutual security concerns, backed by international guarantees. A region at stake Assab represents a test of the future political and security order in the Horn of Africa, with implications far beyond the fate of a port. Ethiopia's need for maritime access is an economic and strategic reality, but turning that need into a claim to sovereignty is no remedy for the underlying economic problem and threatens to ignite a fresh dispute over borders and legitimacy. For Eritrea, defending independence and sovereignty is compatible with establishing good economic relations with its larger neighbour. For the countries of the Horn of Africa, not least Sudan, preventing war is essential to protecting their own security and sovereignty. In a region exhausted by conflict and the collapse of state institutions, the greatest danger is that an attempt to change Ethiopia's landlocked status by force ignites another war, at a cost to all concerned far greater than any benefit its proponents hope to gain. + / - SAVE SHARE Related topics Tigray Ethiopia Eritrea Red Sea Port international trade Horn of Africa Sudan Related Articles The leaders of Egypt, Somalia, Sudan and Eritrea met in Alamein Egypt on 4 October to discuss regional tensions. Civilian accounts from the Amhara, Oromia, Wolaita, and Southwest Ethiopia regions detail a pattern of forced recruitment, arbitrary street detentions, and enforced disappearances. Security forces and kebele militias systematically target young men in urban centers, transit hubs, and rural districts—particularly individuals unable to produce state identity documents. Witnesses report that recruitment operations frequently occur after dusk or in public gathering spaces, including football venues, coffee stalls, and roadside checkpoints, with victims loaded onto military buses and transported to undisclosed holding facilities or training camps. In Sodo within the Wolaita Zone, as well as across districts in South Wollo and Debre Birhan, residents report self-imposed curfews and severe restrictions on daily movement to evade patrol units. Witnesses in Southeast Arsi’s Lude Hetosa woreda described forced sweeps where minors under 18, orphans, and migrant daily laborers were rounded up to fulfill local kebele recruitment quotas without family notification or formal administrative review. While ground sources in Mizan Aman and Wolaita note that public outcry and media scrutiny have led to a temporary decrease in sweep operations in select localities, fear remains pervasive among youth, who describe the recruitment as effectively irreversible disappearance. Anonymous defense personnel acknowledged ongoing recruitment activities but claimed no central government order had been issued for forced conscription. somalia.content: UN Political Mission Closes in Somalia as Constitutional Dispute Remains Unresolved - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS UN Political Mission Closes in Somalia as Constitutional Dispute Remains Unresolved Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Sunday November 1, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — The United Nations ended its political mission in Somalia on Saturday, withdrawing from a role it had played for more than three decades in mediating disputes among the country’s leaders, even as the government and opposition remain at odds over constitutional changes and the timing of the next elections. The departure leaves Somalia without an agreed international mechanism to help resolve a dispute over whether President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud and parliament can remain in office until 2027. The government says constitutional amendments provide a legal basis for the extended terms. Opposition leaders reject that interpretation. The United Nations Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia, known as UNTMIS, formally concluded its operations after a two-year transition intended to transfer its responsibilities to Somali institutions and other UN agencies. The closure marks the end of a succession of UN political missions that began in the early 1990s, following the collapse of Somalia’s central government. Over the years, those missions helped convene negotiations among rival leaders, facilitated agreements on power-sharing and supported efforts to resolve election disputes. Their involvement did not eliminate Somalia’s recurring political crises, but it provided a channel through which competing factions could negotiate, often with international assistance. No comparable mediation framework has been established to replace that role, according to Al Jazeera, leaving the government and opposition to seek a settlement through direct negotiations. The federal government maintains that constitutional amendments adopted under Mohamud’s administration allow the president and members of parliament to remain in office until 2027. Opposition groups dispute that position, arguing against extending the current leadership’s tenure. Mohamud has invited opposition figures to talks aimed at resolving the dispute, but major opposition groups have not confirmed whether they will participate. The mission’s closure followed a request by the Somali government in 2024 to end the UN’s direct political role in the country. Government officials had accused the organisation of interfering in domestic affairs and sought greater Somali responsibility for political and institutional matters. The transition gradually transferred the mission’s responsibilities to national institutions and other parts of the UN system. The withdrawal does not end the UN’s presence in Somalia. Its humanitarian and development agencies will continue operating, although their mandates do not include the political mediation previously undertaken by the mission. Neither the government nor the opposition has announced an agreed procedure for resolving the constitutional dispute, and no alternative mediator has been formally designated if direct negotiations fail. Major opposition groups have yet to confirm whether they will accept Mohamud’s invitation to talks on the constitutional dispute and election timetable. somalia.content: Somalia’s security transition faces major test as international support comes under pressure – People Daily x Search GO Search... ePaper Search GO News Politics Business Insights Advertisement Insights Somalia’s security transition faces major test as international support comes under pressure Sunday 01st November, 2026 06:43 PM | By Kenneth Mwenda Members of Somalia-based Islamist insurgent group Al Shabaab. PHOTO/@DalsanTv/X Somalia’s efforts to take full responsibility for its security are facing a major test as the country navigates a changing international military presence, political divisions and persistent attacks by Al-Shabaab. The closure of the United Nations Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNTMIS) on October 31, 2026, and Uganda’s announcement that it has started withdrawing troops after 20 years in the country have brought renewed attention to the challenges facing the security transition. The developments come as questions persist over the financing and logistical support of the African Union Support and Stabilisation Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM), which continues to support Somali forces in the fight against Al-Shabaab. A policy paper published by Balqiis Insights in July 2026 warned that Somalia could lose security gains if responsibility is transferred to national forces before the country has adequate financing, logistical support and political coordination. The report, titled No Time to Drift: Somalia and the Deadline for a Managed Security Transition , was written by Mustafa Osman and Samira Gaid. It argued that the transition required more than reducing the number of foreign troops or transferring responsibilities to Somali institutions. The authors warned that the country needed a clear plan to sustain military operations and ensure that Somali forces could hold territory reclaimed from Al-Shabaab. “A rapid loss of UNSOS support does not automatically translate to Somali self-reliance,” the paper stated. The warning comes at a time when Somalia is expected to assume greater responsibility for its security while continuing to depend on international partners for military and logistical assistance. AUSSOM’s logistical challenge One of the biggest concerns highlighted in the report is the dependence of AUSSOM on the United Nations Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS). While UNTMIS was responsible for political engagement, governance support and reconciliation, UNSOS provides logistical and operational assistance to African Union troops. The closure of the political mission does not mean that the separate support office has also closed. UNSOS provides essential services, including fuel, food, water, medical care, casualty evacuation, transport, aviation support, communications and engineering services. These services allow AU troops to operate across Somalia and support national forces in military operations against Al-Shabaab. Somalia President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud.PHOTO/https://www.facebook.com/HassanSheikhMahmud The Balqiis Insights paper estimated the UNSOS budget for the 2025/2026 financial year at approximately $537.2 million (Ksh69.6 billion), compared with between $166.5 million and $190 million (Ksh21.6 billion and Ksh24.6 billion) for AUSSOM, using an indicative exchange rate of Ksh129.57 to the dollar. The difference highlights the scale of logistical support required to keep the AU mission operational. The report warned that without a replacement arrangement, AUSSOM could struggle to maintain its operational capacity, even if its mandate remains in place. The financing question became more pressing after the United States indicated in July that it would not support the continuation of the existing UN logistical arrangement beyond the current authorisation period. In September, Reuters reported that Washington had agreed to a 12-month wind-down of logistical support, with the process expected to begin in January 2027. The proposal would allow time for the arrangement to be phased out rather than ending all support immediately on December 31, 2026. However, the proposed wind-down leaves Somalia and its partners with the challenge of finding alternative financing and logistical arrangements to sustain AUSSOM. The Balqiis report identified the absence of an agreed replacement for UNSOS as one of the major gaps in the security transition. Political divisions complicate transition The report also raised concerns about the lack of agreement among Somalia’s political leaders on the country’s security priorities. Disagreements between the federal government and regional administrations have complicated efforts to coordinate security operations and build a common approach to the transfer of responsibilities. Political tensions have also been heightened by disagreements over constitutional changes, election timelines and the distribution of power between Mogadishu and regional states. These divisions could affect intelligence sharing, military planning and cooperation between different security institutions. The closure of UNTMIS also removes a political mission that had supported dialogue, reconciliation and engagement between Somali leaders. The UN has maintained that its broader presence in Somalia will continue through its agencies, funds and programmes. However, humanitarian and development assistance does not automatically replace the political coordination and mediation functions previously carried out by UNTMIS. At the ceremony marking the end of the mission, Raisedon Zenenga, the UN Secretary-General’s Deputy Special Representative for Somalia, acknowledged the progress made but warned that significant challenges remained. “However, continued engagement by the international community will remain important to sustaining progress and addressing outstanding priorities,” Zenenga said. somalia.content: Somalia Gains Duty-Free Access to EU Market Under Trade Scheme - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Somalia Gains Duty-Free Access to EU Market Under Trade Scheme Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Sunday November 1, 2026 Brussels (HOL) — Somali producers are eligible to sell qualifying goods in European Union markets without paying import duties or facing export-volume quotas, under a preferential trade arrangement that could help local businesses expand their overseas sales. The arrangement gives Somali exporters a potential cost advantage when competing in European markets, but businesses must still meet EU product standards and import requirements before their goods can enter the bloc. The EU Delegation to Somalia said in a social media statement that Somalia is among 33 African countries benefiting from the Everything But Arms (EBA) initiative, which provides duty-free and quota-free market access to countries classified among the world's least developed economies. The scheme covers eligible products except arms and ammunition, allowing qualifying shipments to enter EU markets without customs duties or restrictions on the quantity exported under the arrangement. For Somali businesses seeking customers abroad, the preferential terms remove two trade barriers that can make exporting more expensive or limit the volume of goods entering foreign markets. The EU Delegation said the arrangement has no fixed expiry date, offering businesses a continuing opportunity to develop export operations and seek customers in Europe. However, the announcement does not represent a newly negotiated trade agreement or an immediate increase in Somali exports. Somalia's access falls under an existing EU trade preference scheme. Export opportunities depend on meeting EU standards Although the arrangement removes tariffs and quotas, Somali producers must still comply with European quality standards and other import regulations. Those requirements remain a major consideration for businesses assessing whether they can sell their products competitively in the European market. Exporters that satisfy the standards could benefit from reduced trade costs and access to customers without the additional burden of EU import duties on qualifying goods. The absence of quotas also means eligible exporters would not face a fixed limit on shipment volumes under the scheme. The EU Delegation presented the arrangement as an opportunity for Somali businesses to expand production and strengthen their presence in international markets. However, any increase in exports would depend on businesses finding buyers, meeting regulatory requirements and developing the capacity to supply European markets. The delegation's statement did not identify particular Somali products expected to benefit, provide figures for existing exports to the EU or estimate how much additional trade the scheme could generate. It also did not announce any new export contracts or investments resulting from the preferential access. somalia.content: Somalia Opens Party Registration for 2027 Elections Amid Opposition Dispute - Hiiraan Online Jobs | Twitter | Somali Links | RSS Dark Mode Hiiraan Online HOME OPINION POLITICS RSS CONTACT US FACEBOOK × OPINION WARARKA MAANTA SPORTS SECURITY POLITICS Privacy Policy Contact Us Jobs advertisements HOME NEWS Somalia Opens Party Registration for 2027 Elections Amid Opposition Dispute Share Facebook Messenger Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Telegram Copy Link Email Font Size A- A A+ Sunday November 1, 2026 Mogadishu (HOL) — Somalia has opened registration for political parties seeking to contest the country's planned 2027 federal elections, moving ahead with preparations for a one-person, one-vote system despite opposition demands for a political agreement on the electoral process. The registration window, which runs from November 1 to November 22, 2026, gives political groups three weeks to apply for participation in elections that would allow Somali voters to choose their parliamentary representatives directly under the commission's proposed framework. The National Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission announced the registration period as part of a timetable that schedules elections for both houses of the Federal Parliament on April 15, 2027, followed by a presidential election on May 15. The commission has also set November 22 as the deadline for submitting parliamentary candidate lists, requiring political groups to complete two major electoral preparations within the same period. Campaigning is scheduled to begin on February 27, 2027. The announcement marks a significant step in preparations for the planned federal elections, but it also brings the commission's timetable into sharper conflict with opposition groups that have rejected the process without a broader political settlement. Opposition challenges electoral framework Somali opposition groups have called for an agreement among political stakeholders before electoral preparations proceed, arguing that outstanding constitutional questions and disputes over the election framework must first be resolved. Their objections raise questions about whether the commission's timetable can secure wider political acceptance before parties begin campaigning. At the centre of the disagreement is the proposed one-person, one-vote system, which the commission intends to use for the federal elections. Under the plan, citizens would vote directly for their parliamentary representatives, replacing the approach to selecting lawmakers with the direct voting arrangements outlined by the commission. Opposition groups, however, maintain that the rules governing the elections and unresolved constitutional issues require political agreement before the process advances. The commission has continued its preparations despite those objections, maintaining the registration deadline and election dates already announced. No agreement resolving the opposition's concerns was identified in the information accompanying the registration announcement. advertisements November deadline puts political parties on the clock The immediate focus now shifts to political groups seeking to participate in the planned elections. They have until November 22 to complete registration, the same deadline established for submitting parliamentary candidate lists. The overlapping deadlines place pressure on parties preparing to enter the electoral process while disagreement continues over the framework under which they would compete. The commission's schedule leaves the period between the November registration deadline and the February 27 campaign launch for further preparations ahead of voting. Parliamentary elections are scheduled for April 15, with the presidential election planned for May 15, 2027. Whether those dates can proceed as planned remains closely tied to the unresolved dispute over electoral rules and constitutional questions. The next immediate test will come on November 22, when the registration and candidate-list deadlines expire, providing an early indication of which political groups are prepared to participate under the commission's proposed arrangements. The broader political question remains whether the commission and opposition stakeholders can reach an agreement before campaigning begins in February, or whether the dispute over the electoral framework will continue into the final months before the planned federal elections. The machines are: - Immunohistochemistry (IHC), which distinguishes between types of cancer - Frozen Section, used for rapid testing during surgery - Liquid-based preparation, a modern method for preparing tissue samples The Pathology department examines body tissues to diagnose disease. Dr. Ismail Mahmoud Abdullahi, head of the hospital's Pathology department, said the IHC machine is vital for cancer treatment. It shows the exact type of cancer, helps doctors choose the right medication, and predicts the patient's future outlook. The Frozen Section machine allows doctors to get results while the patient is still on the operating table. A small piece of tissue is taken and examined immediately. The test shows whether cancer remains at the edges of the removed tissue. It also shows whether the cancer has spread to the lymph nodes, as in breast cancer. These results determine how extensive the surgery needs to be. Dr. Ismail said the machine is also important for children with Hirschsprung disease, a condition children are born with in which part of the intestine lacks the nerves that move it, causing severe constipation. These children used to wait two to three weeks for their results from abroad. They now receive results within 20 minutes. "It will reduce the many surgeries and the hardship patients faced," he said. The equipment arrives at a time when cancer is a major challenge to Somali communities. Somalia does not have a national cancer registry. Data presented at the Somali Success Forum showed that 6,128 cancer cases were registered between 2023 and 2026. Cancer is the most common illness for which Somalis travel abroad for treatment.
